topics.summary: The gateway accepts a job and then crashes. After restart, the caller asks whether the job exists. If acceptance was only a message in memory, the service has lost an externally visible promise. If acceptance was committed in durable state, the process can recover its obligation even though its threads, sockets, and counters disappeared.

topics.title: 14.2.1 Wrapping Connections, Statements, and Transactions
topics.summary: A connection owns the database handle. A prepared statement owns its compiled statement handle. A transaction object owns the responsibility to roll back unless commit succeeds. These are separate lifetimes and should appear as separate RAII types or equally explicit scopes.

cards.question: Explain Wrapping Connections, Statements, and Transactions in your own words.

topics.title: 14.3.1 Interpreting WAL and Synchronous Settings
topics.summary: Write-ahead logging changes how updates and readers interact. Readers can observe a consistent snapshot while committed changes are represented in the WAL, and checkpointing later transfers appropriate pages into the main database. It does not make SQLite a multi-writer distributed storage system. (R19, R20)

topics.title: 14.3.2 Testing Reopen, Rollback, and Concurrent Requests
topics.summary: An in-memory database is useful for fast logic tests, but it disappears with its connection and does not test process recovery. The companion therefore also creates private file-backed databases, closes and reopens them, and verifies retained rows and receipt counts.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Success is returned before commit
topics.summary: If the handler sends ACCEPTED before transaction commit, a later commit failure can erase the promise the client already received. Reordering the response after commit closes that particular gap. It does not guarantee the client receives the response; a lost reply remains possible after a successful commit.

blocks.text: The store begins an immediate transaction before checking the receipt. One writer obtains the transaction first. It sees no row, inserts the receipt, and commits. The other writer waits according to the configured bounded busy policy, then examines the now-existing row and returns the matching saved result. If contention exceeds that policy, it can fail visibly and be retried safely later with the same identity.

reading.title: Engineering case — Explain two connections racing on the same key
paragraphs: Two worker connections receive EXEC same42 9 nearly together. Each intends to create a receipt for the same canonical request. The required outcome is one retained receipt and the same result returned to both callers, not two independent records or an unexplained error for the second caller.

The store begins an immediate transaction before checking the receipt. One writer obtains the transaction first. It sees no row, inserts the receipt, and commits. The other writer waits according to the configured bounded busy policy, then examines the now-existing row and returns the matching saved result. If contention exceeds that policy, it can fail visibly and be retried safely later with the same identity.

Now change the second request to input 10. It must not receive the saved result for input 9 as if its new work succeeded. The existing row is compared with canonical meaning, and the conflict is reported. The unique key constraint prevents duplication; the application comparison prevents meaning from being overwritten or confused.

A check outside the transaction would not provide the same reasoning. Both connections could observe absence and then race to insert. The constraint would still prevent two rows, but the losing path would need careful error interpretation and a fresh lookup. Keeping the read-check-write decision inside the transaction makes the intended result easier to follow.

The busy timeout is a bound on one database waiting mechanism, not a guarantee that the entire request completes within that many milliseconds. Scheduling, I/O, statement execution, and response transfer add other costs. The reactor’s handler can block while the database waits, which is explicitly documented rather than hidden behind nonblocking socket terminology.

The test uses two connections against a private file-backed database and verifies receipt count and returned results. It provides stronger evidence for this local contention path than an in-memory single-connection test. It still does not establish behavior for every filesystem, storage device, or distributed database engine.

The general lesson is to make the serializing authority explicit. In this lab it is SQLite’s transaction and uniqueness machinery over one file. Replacing that file with two independent copies removes the authority even if both copies retain exactly the same C++ wrapper code.
